(9000, 1, '2025-09-15 14:25:44', '2025-09-15 12:25:44', '', 'stock-photo', 'The Hidden Burden of Living with Eczema\niStock Photo', 'inherit', 'open', 'closed', '', 'stock-photo', '', '', '2025-09-15 14:26:10', '2025-09-15 12:26:10', '', 9001, 'https://bushnews.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/stock-photo.webp', 0, 'attachment', 'image/webp', 0),
(9001, 15, '2025-09-15 14:20:00', '2025-09-15 12:20:00', '<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>In many black communities, eczema is often misunderstood, dismissed as “just dry skin” or even linked to myths about poor hygiene. Yet for those who live with it, the condition is far more complex, painful and emotionally draining.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Eczema, or atopic dermatitis, is a chronic skin condition that causes itching, dryness and inflamed patches. On darker skin tones, it may appear grey, purple or dark brown rather than red, which can make diagnosis difficult and lead to under-treatment. This hidden nature of eczema often adds to the struggle.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>A Silent Struggle</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For children in townships and villages, eczema can be especially tough. The constant itching disturbs sleep, leaving them tired at school. Some parents share stories of being told by relatives that their child’s skin problems are due to “bad blood” or “not bathing properly.” These misconceptions can add guilt and shame to what is already a challenging condition.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Adults, too, often carry the hidden burden. Many cover up their arms and legs, even in summer, to avoid questions or stares. The pressure to appear strong and “presentable” in the workplace or at social gatherings means the emotional impact is rarely spoken about, despite it being very real.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Beyond the Skin</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The toll of eczema goes deeper than the surface. People living with the condition often report anxiety, low self-esteem and feelings of isolation. For black women in particular, who already face societal pressures around beauty and appearance, eczema can feel like an extra layer of judgment.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Steps Towards Support</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Awareness is key. More healthcare professionals are now being trained to recognise how skin conditions present differently on black skin, but communities also need to play their part. By rejecting stigma and offering support, families and neighbours can help those with eczema feel seen and understood.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Simple acts, such as encouraging children not to tease classmates or creating safe spaces for adults to talk openly, can break the silence around this condition.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Eczema is not a matter of poor care or neglect. Their lives must change now,” the party stressed.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The EFF called for a staggering R10 billion to be set aside exclusively for Bushbuckridge to address unemployment and service delivery failures. The DA, on the other hand, demanded an urgent investigation into why many communities remain excluded from electrification projects. The party proposed a 21-day deadline for a preliminary report with practical recommendations to ensure schools, clinics and households receive access to electricity without further delays.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:gallery {\"linkTo\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-gallery has-nested-images columns-default is-cropped\"><!-- wp:image {\"id\":9068,\"sizeSlug\":\"large\",\"linkDestination\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-image size-large\"><img src=\"https://bushnews.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/IMG_7875-scaled-1-1200x900.jpeg\" alt=\"\" class=\"wp-image-9068\"/></figure>\n<!-- /wp:image -->\n\n<!-- wp:image {\"id\":9067,\"sizeSlug\":\"large\",\"linkDestination\":\"none\"} -->\n<figure class=\"wp-block-image size-large\"><img src=\"https://bushnews.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/IMG_7885-1200x900.jpeg\" alt=\"\" class=\"wp-image-9067\"/></figure>\n<!-- /wp:image --></figure>\n<!-- /wp:gallery -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>In his closing address, Mpumalanga Premier Mandla Ndlovu acknowledged residents’ frustrations but dismissed the EFF’s proposal as unrealistic. He said:</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>“The budget of the province is 67, a billion. So we don’t have, for infrastructure, in the program, the budget is not even 10 billion. So they know that it is not possible. I wish I can be like them. If you are not in government, you can even promise people to build one million houses in the 1st 5 years. That’s what we did. I don’t understand why they decided to lie, knowing that they are lying, but they continue to lie. So it is not right. Ourselves, we should not be ambitious. We must tell people what we can be able to meet. So don’t come with ambitious program that we will not be able to make.”</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Premier Ndlovu reassured communities that access to water, roads, and electricity remains a government priority. He confirmed that household connections are underway, with newly established stands also scheduled to be connected. On unemployment, he pointed to local manufacturing projects such as GNG Welding, which has already created 14 jobs, as a model for sustainable growth.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Bushbuckridge by Numbers</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>· 11.2% of households lack running water</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>· 28,000 houses are urgently needed</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>· 1,500 toilets budgeted for Bushbuckridge South</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>· 97 graveyards without fencing</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>· 1.9% of residents live in informal settlements</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>As the dust settled at Ximungwe, one reality remained: Bushbuckridge’s 38 wards demand more than political theatre. (9296, 15, '2025-10-03 12:30:11', '2025-10-03 10:30:11', '<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The Constitutional Court has ruled that fathers are now entitled to the same parental leave as mothers, marking a historic step towards gender equality in South Africa’s workplace policies.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The court found that the current law was discriminatory and unconstitutional, as it unfairly limited fathers’ role in childcare. Until now, the Basic Conditions of Employment Act granted mothers four months of maternity leave, while fathers were restricted to just ten days.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>In its judgment, the court emphasised that the law perpetuated the outdated view that women should be the primary caregivers. (9582, 15, '2025-10-28 08:10:00', '2025-10-28 06:10:00', '<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>South Africa has made history as the first African country to approve a long-acting injection to prevent HIV. The South African Health Products Regulatory Authority (SAHPRA) announced on 27 October that it had registered <em>lenacapavir</em>, developed by global pharmaceutical company Gilead Sciences.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Unlike daily tablets, the injection is given only twice a year. The SCA ruled that such practices contravene the <strong>Gauteng Gambling Act of 1995</strong> and reaffirmed the principle that each mode of gambling—casinos, betting, limited payout machines, and bingo—must be licensed and regulated separately.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>According to the judgment, casino games cannot be classified as “events or occurrences” for betting purposes under the <strong>National Gambling Act of 2004</strong>. This means that bookmakers who offer such games are effectively operating casinos illegally.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The NGB described this as an “unfair practice”, highlighting that licensed casinos face stricter tax obligations and regulatory controls compared to bookmakers. “The ruling affirms that interactive gambling remains unlawful in South Africa,” said Acting Chief Executive Officer, Mr Dukwana.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The Board warned that any bookmaker found offering unlawful casino-style betting could face serious consequences. Under the National Gambling Act, the NGB has the power to <strong>confiscate winnings from illegal gambling activities</strong>. Offenders also face criminal sanctions, including fines of up to <strong>R10 million</strong> or imprisonment of up to <strong>ten years</strong>.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Mr Dukwana called on all <strong>Provincial Licensing Authorities</strong> to tighten oversight of their licensees and act swiftly in cases of non-compliance. “We urge bookmakers to comply fully with the law and refrain from practices that undermine the integrity of the gambling industry,” he said.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The ruling has implications beyond Gauteng, extending to all bookmakers nationwide. (9754, 15, '2025-11-10 15:30:00', '2025-11-10 13:30:00', '<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>It is not often that a man openly declares his decision to postpone fatherhood until he is completely ready for the responsibility. The notion of a man deliberately delaying fatherhood is therefore unusual and even frowned upon in some circles. Yet Mashabela’s choice compels society to rethink what responsible parenthood really means. Waiting until one is ready may appear unconventional, but it can also reflect maturity, foresight and self-discipline.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Many men feel enormous pressure to conform to social expectations. In cultures where fatherhood is viewed as a rite of passage, those who delay it are sometimes seen as avoiding responsibility. (9919, 15, '2025-11-20 17:00:00', '2025-11-20 15:00:00', '<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Mbombela – Mpumalanga has officially launched its first-ever provincial Roll Call, bringing together all traffic law enforcement officers ahead of what is expected to be one of the busiest and most demanding festive seasons. The historic gathering, held at Mbombela Stadium on Thursday, 20 November 2025, featured a powerful address by MEC for Community Safety, Security and Liaison, Mr Jackie Macie, and a keynote speech by Deputy Minister of Transport, Mr Mkhuleko Hlengwa.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The event drew Executive Mayors from across all districts, senior SAPS officials, municipal MMCs, transport stakeholders including BUSCOR and the Border Management Authority, as well as hundreds of provincial and municipal traffic officers.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 class=\"wp-block-heading\">MEC Macie: ‘Visibility Is Non-Negotiable’</h3>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>MEC Macie said the Roll Call marks the beginning of an annual tradition that will precede each festive season. He thanked officers for their dedication and reminded them of their immense responsibility.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>“You are the face of safety on our roads,” Macie said. “Your presence, discipline, courage and sacrifices save lives in our province.”</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>He revealed that Mpumalanga recorded 742 crashes and 143 fatalities during the previous festive season—slightly lower than the previous year—and stressed that the province is committed to halving road deaths by 2030, in line with the United Nations’ targets.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>To achieve this, Macie announced intensified operations from Thursdays through Mondays, with additional corridor operations during peak travel periods. Survivors are withdrawing cases because they fear secondary victimisation more than the perpetrators themselves,” said Nomalanga Ngwenya, Project Manager for Gender Justice in Mpumalanga.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>According to the memorandum, LGBTQIA+ people — particularly women, trans and gender-diverse individuals — face heightened risks of violence, which are worsened when survivors encounter biased questioning, a lack of empathy or inadequate protection from the police.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Caroline Sibuyi, organiser of the LGBTQIA+ Bushbuckridge sector, said the march was not only about visibility but also about demanding dignity.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>“I feel happy and very positive about the march because we wanted Bushbuckridge residents and police officers to see that we exist and can stand together as the LGBTIQ+ community. -->\n<li>Withdrawal of Cases: Fear, intimidation and lack of trust continue to drive high case-withdrawal rates.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Protection of Survivors: There is an urgent need for stronger, survivor-centred reporting and investigation protocols.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>\n<!-- /wp:list -->\n\n<!-- wp:heading {\"level\":3} -->\n<h3 understanding of LGBTQIA+ issues and reduce discriminatory behaviour.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Creation of Safe Spaces: LGBTQIA+-friendly reporting areas within police stations where survivors can seek help without judgement.</li>\n<!-- /wp:list-item -->\n\n<!-- wp:list-item -->\n<li>Increased Awareness and Outreach: Encouraging survivors to report cases by (10046, 15, '2025-12-02 16:21:59', '2025-12-02 14:21:59', '<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The Border Management Authority (BMA) has confirmed the interception of a large consignment of illegally imported veterinary medicines at Polokwane International Airport on 26 November 2025. The seizure forms part of intensified efforts to protect South Africa’s livestock industry amid ongoing Foot and Mouth Disease (FMD) outbreaks.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>According to BMA Commissioner Dr Michael Masiapato, Port Agriculture officials intercepted an aircraft arriving from Kenya and Tanzania carrying veterinary medicines known as <em>Berenil</em>. The products were found packed in two polystyrene boxes with a combined weight of approximately 84 kilograms. The shipment was reportedly in transit to Pietermaritzburg Airport.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The consignment was denied entry after officials established that it lacked the legally required import permits under Section 6 of the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984. Following consultations with the Department of Agriculture, the medicines were confiscated and sent to the Onderstepoort Veterinary Institute – Transboundary Animal Diseases Laboratory (OVI-TAD) for further analysis.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Commissioner Masiapato emphasised the BMA’s vigilance, noting the serious biosecurity threat posed by the illegal importation of veterinary products, particularly during the ongoing FMD outbreak. He said strengthened inspections at ports of entry are essential to safeguarding the health of the national herd and protecting the economic stability of local farmers.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The attempt to smuggle untested animal medicines is considered a serious violation of South Africa’s veterinary and biosecurity laws. Foot and Mouth Disease is a highly contagious viral illness affecting cattle, sheep, goats and pigs, with severe consequences for livestock production and international trade.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>There are seven serotypes of the FMD virus, each requiring a specific vaccine. The introduction of foreign serotypes could compromise the Department of Agriculture’s ongoing control measures. Only legally procured FMD vaccines, sourced from the Botswana Vaccine Institute, are permitted for use in South Africa.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Farmers have been urged to contact their local State Veterinarian if they suspect any signs of FMD in their livestock. Authorities have reiterated that unauthorised use of vaccines remains strictly prohibited.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The BMA’s Port Agriculture unit remains committed to supporting national disease control programmes and strengthening South Africa’s biosecurity.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Members of the public are encouraged to report corruption, suspicious activity or smuggling attempts through <strong>Operation HI-TIVISE</strong> on <strong>0801 229 019</strong>, or via the BMA website at <strong><a href=\"http://www.bma.gov.za\">www.bma.gov.za</a></strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->', 'Illegal Veterinary Medicines Seized at Polokwane Airport', '', 'publish', 'open', 'open', '', 'illegal-veterinary-medicines-seized-at-polokwane-airport', '', '', '2025-12-02 16:22:57', '2025-12-02 14:22:57', '', 0, 'https://bushnews.co.za/illegal-veterinary-medicines-seized-at-polokwane-airport/', 0, 'post', '', 0),
(10047, 1, '2025-12-02 16:22:57', '2025-12-02 14:22:57', '<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The Border Management Authority (BMA) has confirmed the interception of a large consignment of illegally imported veterinary medicines at Polokwane International Airport on 26 November 2025. The seizure forms part of intensified efforts to protect South Africa’s livestock industry amid ongoing Foot and Mouth Disease (FMD) outbreaks.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>According to BMA Commissioner Dr Michael Masiapato, Port Agriculture officials intercepted an aircraft arriving from Kenya and Tanzania carrying veterinary medicines known as <em>Berenil</em>. The products were found packed in two polystyrene boxes with a combined weight of approximately 84 kilograms. The shipment was reportedly in transit to Pietermaritzburg Airport.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The consignment was denied entry after officials established that it lacked the legally required import permits under Section 6 of the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984. Following consultations with the Department of Agriculture, the medicines were confiscated and sent to the Onderstepoort Veterinary Institute – Transboundary Animal Diseases Laboratory (OVI-TAD) for further analysis.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Commissioner Masiapato emphasised the BMA’s vigilance, noting the serious biosecurity threat posed by the illegal importation of veterinary products, particularly during the ongoing FMD outbreak. He said strengthened inspections at ports of entry are essential to safeguarding the health of the national herd and protecting the economic stability of local farmers.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The attempt to smuggle untested animal medicines is considered a serious violation of South Africa’s veterinary and biosecurity laws. Foot and Mouth Disease is a highly contagious viral illness affecting cattle, sheep, goats and pigs, with severe consequences for livestock production and international trade.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>There are seven serotypes of the FMD virus, each requiring a specific vaccine. The introduction of foreign serotypes could compromise the Department of Agriculture’s ongoing control measures. Only legally procured FMD vaccines, sourced from the Botswana Vaccine Institute, are permitted for use in South Africa.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>Farmers have been urged to contact their local State Veterinarian if they suspect any signs of FMD in their livestock. The initiative, unveiled on Tuesday 9 December 2025, is a collaboration between Petco, the Kruger National Park Honorary Rangers amongst others and aims to boost recycling efforts while protecting the park’s fragile environment.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>With more than 270,000 visitors expected, waste generation is a major concern. The new system—also known as the Green Crew—separates recyclables from food and organic waste, as well as general non-recyclable rubbish. Her visit to the Russian State Library was another highlight — an experience she describes as unforgettable and rich with lessons for the South African publishing space.</strong></p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p><strong>Although there are no formal expansion plans into Eastern Europe yet, Njongo believes the seeds of collaboration are already planted. (10683, 15, '2026-02-19 09:48:22', '2026-02-19 07:48:22', '<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>A new University of the Free State (UFS) study is raising fresh questions about what South Africans may be exposed to during their monthly cycle. The team screened for three groups of endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs): <strong>phthalates, bisphenols (including BPA), and parabens</strong>.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>The results showed widespread contamination across all products tested. <strong>Bisphenols were detected in 100% of pads and 75% of pantyliners</strong>, while <strong>parabens were found in over 81% of pads and 75% of liners</strong>. <strong>Phthalates appeared in all pantyliners tested</strong> and in <strong>50% of sanitary pads</strong>. Researchers said these chemicals may not always be added on purpose, but could migrate into products through plastics, adhesives, inks, and manufacturing processes.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>What makes this issue especially personal is where these products are used. Menstrual pads and liners come into contact with <strong>mucosal tissue</strong>, which can absorb chemicals more directly than normal skin. In South Africa, standards focus largely on performance and hygiene, but researchers say there are <strong>limited chemical standards</strong> for the substances detected, and manufacturers are generally <strong>not required to disclose full ingredient lists</strong>.</p>\n<!-- /wp:paragraph -->\n\n<!-- wp:paragraph -->\n<p>For consumers, the advice is practical rather than panic-driven: look for products with independent certification such as <strong>OEKO-TEX Standard 100</strong>, and consider <strong>reusable alternatives</strong> where suitable.
